title: A Coupled Thermomechanical Model with Volterra Memory: Influence of the Kernel Class on Relaxation Asymptotics
authors: Andrii Siasiev
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33185v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The aim of this study is to determine how the class and asymptotic behaviour of a Volterra memory kernel influence relaxation in a coupled thermomechanical model. The model describes the mutual interaction between an internal mechanical variable and temperature through temperature-dependent material properties and mechanical dissipation. The analysis combines a Volterra integral formulation, a spectral representation of the memory mechanism, thermodynamic decomposition of the hereditary power, local well-posedness analysis, linearization near equilibrium, and Laplace-transform asymptotic arguments. The spectral representation separates the energy stored in the relaxation modes from irreversible hereditary dissipation and establishes the thermodynamic consistency of the memory contribution. Under minimal assumptions on the constitutive functions and the kernel, local existence and uniqueness of solutions are obtained; for thermodynamically dissipative memory and a non-negative external heat source, positivity of the absolute temperature is preserved. The main result concerns the linearized dynamics near equilibrium: with the thermomechanical coupling kept unchanged, an exponential kernel produces exponential relaxation, whereas a power-law kernel with a long tail produces algebraic relaxation. A numerical comparison performed for the same set of dimensionless thermomechanical parameters illustrates these two asymptotic regimes. The results show that changing the class of the memory kernel alone can change the qualitative long-time relaxation law of the coupled system.

title: Time-reflection nonlocal equations from $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$-symmetric oscillator pairs: physical origin and variational formulation
authors: Ilmar Gahramanov, Ya\u{g}{\i}zhan \c{S}ahin
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33186v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show that every second-order differential equation with time reflection describes the $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$-symmetric solutions of a local pair of oscillators that is invariant under exchange combined with time reversal. For linear equations the pair is built from springs, balanced gain and loss, and a gyroscopic coupling. We determine when such a pair has a regular first-order Lagrangian, and when the solutions of the equation fix its coefficients. As the main example, we consider a recently studied equation whose solutions do not depend on its velocity coupling. In the corresponding pair this coupling acts only on the conserved total momentum, which vanishes for $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$-symmetric solutions, and each of the two conditions that single out the model places the pair at an exceptional point. When the spring and velocity couplings are both nonzero, the pair has no regular first-order Lagrangian, while the equation has one with second derivatives. We also propose an electronic realization and construct a Bateman-type Hamiltonian, from which the velocity coupling is removed by a canonical transformation.

title: A computer-assisted proof of one-cell snaking and lattice trapping for a nonlinear square lattice
authors: Jiangchao Qian
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33208v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We establish a computer-assisted proof of lattice trapping in an infinite nonlinear square lattice with interaction potential $\phi(t)=(1-e^{-3t^2})/6$ and an antiplane crack far field $K\sqrt{r}\sin(\theta/2)$. We construct a connected branch of equilibria whose single-cell segment contains exactly two nondegenerate quadratic folds, with a stability sequence of stable, Morse index one, and stable in the full energy space. The fold loads satisfy $0.45897<0.45923$ and $0.46219<0.46242$, establishing a strictly positive lattice-trapping width $K_+-K_->0.00296$. A uniqueness argument establishes exact translation closure and smooth continuation across lattice cells. The proof combines renormalized energy, Schur complement estimates, analytic infinite-tail bounds, interval arithmetic, and exact integer positivity certificates. All finite input data, verification programs, and recorded certificate outputs are provided in the accompanying certificate archive.

title: Syringe reuse in HCV transmission among people who inject drugs: behavioral thresholds and optimal control
authors: Mohammad Zaman, Emel Khan, Ishfaq Ahmad, Hiromi Seno
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33222v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) transmission among people who inject drugs (PWID) is driven largely by syringe sharing and reuse, yet existing models rarely treat reuse as a behavior that individuals adopt and abandon. In this work, we develop and analyze a four-compartment epidemic model that explicitly incorporates syringe reuse as a distinct behavioral process, introducing a high-risk susceptible subgroup that acquires infection through both direct contact and syringe-mediated transmission. We establish the well-posedness and biological feasibility of the model, derive the basic reproduction number, and analyze the existence and stability of the disease-free and endemic equilibria along with closed-form behavioral threshold conditions for syringe-reuse adoption and cessation. Global sensitivity and scenario analyses reveal that while transmission and recovery parameters dominate epidemic potential, behavioral parameters governing the adoption and cessation of syringe reuse play a crucial role in disease persistence and control thresholds. The model's projected infection dynamics are broadly consistent with observed U.S. HCV incidence trends. We further formulate an optimal control problem targeting reuse initiation and cessation, and show through cost-effectiveness analysis that combined behavioral interventions outperform single-component strategies in reducing both infection and high-risk behavior. These results indicate that behavioral prevention aimed at syringe reuse is a necessary component of sustained HCV control among PWID.

title: Bistable waves and propagation success on hexagonal lattice
authors: Jian Fang, Yifei Li, Yijun Lou, Jian Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33224v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inspired by propagation phenomena occurring on media with hexagonal structures, we propose an idealized system of bistable reaction-diffusion equations posed on a hexagonal lattice, and investigate the existence and speed of traveling wave solutions. We establish a sharp criterion for propagation success (nonzero wave speed) and failure (zero wave speed), where the criterion is determined by an angle-dependent periodic threshold function and the ratio of two parameters in the nonlinearity. Moreover, the sign of the wave speeds is governed by the angle and the parameter ratio. Our results imply that the hexagonal structure and bistability significantly affect the propagation dynamics.

title: Quantization concealment of angular momentum: dynamic origin of spins
authors: Wenjie Long, Wei Ku
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33267v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Since their introduction, spins of elementary particles remain a phenomenological addition to modern quantum theories. While relatively recent studies on Dirac and other linearized equations of motion have revealed the spatial current nature of the spin magnetic moment (instead of the commonly pictured self-rotation), the dynamical origin of this circulating current remains unresolved. Here, we expose a long-overlooked generic shortcoming of wave mechanics ("quantization concealment of angular momentum") that undesirably reduces the canonical angular momentum of bound eigen-modes and renders incomplete the minimal coupling to magnetic fields. Recovering the kinetic orbital angular momentum resolves $1s$-orbital's counterintuitive "zero" angular momentum and reproduces all planar modes' anomalous Zeeman splitting. Regarding spins as effective remedy to the concealment offers natural explanations to their main puzzles: 1) dynamical origin of spin magnetic moment and 2) frame invariance of spin angular momentum. This implies absence of spin magnetic moment for free particles, a strong prediction verifiable through Stern-Gerlach experiments on electrons.

title: Sharp one-shot bounds and optimal exponents of universal randomness extraction
authors: Bartosz Regula, Hao-Chung Cheng
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce techniques for the study of randomness extraction against quantum side information (privacy amplification) by relating this problem to variants of hypothesis testing tasks with quadratic constraints. Building also on the recently introduced measured smooth entropy approach of [Regula and Tomamichel, arXiv:2603.04493], we precisely determine the optimal scaling of the error of quantum privacy amplification in several regimes. Our results apply to the standard operational security criterion based on trace distance and focus in particular on universal classes of hash functions. On the technical side, our investigation reveals connections with operator space theory methods used in non-commutative Khintchine inequalities. As one application, we give a one-shot converse bound that shows the leftover hash lemma of [arXiv:2603.04493] to be tight up to a constant factor for all strongly 4-universal hash functions. This allows us to evaluate the asymptotic i.i.d. error exponent of universal randomness extraction for all rates, matching the bound of [Dupuis, arXiv:2105.05342] and improving also earlier classical asymptotic results of [Hayashi, arXiv:1010.1358]. We furthermore give new one-shot achievability and converse bounds on the error in the strong converse regime, which we show to match up to a constant factor. This establishes the exact strong converse exponent of quantum privacy amplification under 2-universal hash functions, complementing the converse bound of [Shen, Gao, and Cheng, arXiv:2202.10263].

title: Theory of Anomalous Diffusion and Superdiffusion in Integrable Spin Chains
authors: Jitendra Kethepalli, Andrew Urilyon, Jacopo De Nardis
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33274v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Integrable systems can exhibit diffusive or Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) scaling in two-point correlations even when their current full counting statistics (FCS) differ from those usually associated with these universality classes. We explain this separation using a multispecies particle gas that preserves the scattering structure of integrable spin chains. For anisotropy $\Delta>1$, large particles are advected by a mobile bath. The resulting FCS has a Gaussian-mixture form and approaches the M-Wright distribution at late times, with finite-time rounding due to mobile species. At the isotropic point $\Delta=1$, all particles are mobile, and the charge transfer by large particles is discrete. A self-consistent Poisson distribution describes the FCS, with a nearly Gaussian bulk and model-dependent, non-Gaussian tails. By contrast, two-point correlations follow from the statistics of a large tracer particle. For $\Delta>1$, it undergoes Brownian motion, yielding Gaussian spreading. At $\Delta=1$, we provide evidence from fluctuating hydrodynamics for the emergence of the KPZ Pr\"ahofer--Spohn scaling function in dynamical correlations and trace it to the finite coupling of the largest particles to a continuum of slower ones, with long-ranged velocity fluctuations. Our framework shows how universal dynamical two-point correlations coexist with distinct model-dependent current statistics.

title: Structure-factor witnesses of thermal entanglement: exact optimal covariance criteria for the XY chain
authors: Julia Math\'e, Ayaka Usui, Otfried G\"uhne, Giuseppe Vitagliano
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33284v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Which entanglement witness is optimal for a thermal many-body state, and what does its structure reveal about the equilibrium physics? We address these questions for the spin-$1/2$ XY chain in a transverse field, using the covariance-matrix criterion (CMC), which requires only one- and two-spin correlations. We show that for thermal states the optimal CMC witness is fixed by the minima over momentum of the three static spin structure factors, which are accessible to scattering experiments and can be evaluated directly in the thermodynamic limit. The optimal witnesses select the collective spin modes with the smallest thermal fluctuations, with their form dictated by symmetry rather than by criticality. They certify entanglement, and can also bound entanglement measures, up to temperatures of the order of the exchange coupling, including in states without any pairwise entanglement. A systematic investigation of entanglement in small chains reveals that the CMC is nearly as powerful as a moment-matrix hierarchy supplied with all spin correlations, and close to the XX point it detects thermal states that are PPT across every bipartition. In addition, we observe that the same witnesses can also certify entanglement generated by a sudden quench from a thermal state in which none is detected.

title: Quditology: harnessing many levels for quantum information processing
authors: Abhijit Chakraborty, Zheng Shi, Noah Goss, Irfan Siddiqi, Barry C. Sanders, Christine A. Muschik
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33299v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum computing offers the prospect of surpassing classical computation on certain tasks by leveraging quantum coherence and entanglement. However, a significant gap remains between current quantum hardware and the requirements to transcend what classical computers can achieve, with decoherence limiting the capacity of storing quantum information and the number of logical steps that can be executed reliably. In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.

title: Gauge symmetry permits extremely low-depth random unitary circuits
authors: Yunfei Wang, Yuqing Li, Junqi Wang, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Junyu Liu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33312v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous global symmetries can obstruct logarithmic-depth symmetric unitary $k$-designs and pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) through long-range correlations. We ask whether gauge symmetries impose analogous limitations. For $\mathrm{U}(1)$ lattice gauge theories, we identify a randomization scale $c$, the minimum patch size needed for matter to screen every allowed boundary-flux mismatch, and a diffusive scale governing boundary-flux correlations. Glued circuits built from gauge-symmetric unitaries with subdiffusive support are efficiently distinguishable from gauge-symmetric Haar-random unitaries, whereas local controlled designs can be glued into global approximate designs when overlaps exceed the diffusive scale multiplied by a logarithmic factor. Our analysis suggests incomplete screening limits design guarantees to constant order, whereas strictly locally random systems with complete local screening ($c=1$) admit a local tensor-product description, permitting superpolynomial design orders and logarithmic-depth designs and PRUs. We construct a toy model of charged black-hole evaporation in which insufficient screening makes uninterrupted complete discharge exponentially unlikely in $c$, whereas strict local randomization removes this screening obstruction. This motivates a quantum-information analogue of the weak gravity conjecture, requiring the available charged spectrum to support complete local screening in addition to superextremality. We conjecture that this condition allows gauge-symmetric systems to scramble as rapidly as unconstrained ones and support this by constructing logarithmic-depth approximate strong designs and strong PRUs.

title: When does a noisy Bell pair attain the Rains bound?
authors: Matthew Barber, Stefano Pirandola
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33317v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Two entangled Bell-diagonal qubit states with the same singlet fraction have the same Rains bound. We prove that their attainable rates under operations preserving the positive partial transpose can nevertheless differ: the bound is attained if and only if one of the Bell probabilities vanishes. Every mixed entangled isotropic state, in every finite dimension, lies strictly below its bound. This refutes the attainment suggested by finite-block numerics, and places the two-way quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel strictly below its relative-entropy bound.

title: Chiral Domain-Wall Modes in Topological Adaptive Quantum Dynamics
authors: Asadullah Bhuiyan, Haining Pan, Chao-Ming Jian
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33328v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum dynamical systems driven by both unitary evolution and measurements open a new landscape of nonequilibrium phases of matter. The role of topology in enriching this landscape remains less understood than that of entanglement and symmetry. A particularly interesting question concerns protected dynamical modes localized on spacetime domain walls between topologically distinct dynamical phases. These dynamical topological domain-wall modes (DTDMs) are well understood only for $0+1$D walls in $1+1$D fermionic dynamics. In this work, we study $1+1$D topological domain walls in $2+1$D charge-conserving free-fermion dynamics, modeled by topological adaptive circuits that steer the two sides of each wall toward a Chern insulator and a trivial insulator through measurements and feedforward corrections. Although the circuits target no particular wall state, each wall hosts $1+1$D chiral DTDMs. At long times in each quantum trajectory, they exhibit logarithmic scaling of entanglement and charge variance and algebraically decaying density correlations, surprisingly consistent with the ground state of a $1+1$D chiral free-fermion conformal field theory. This contrasts with purely $1+1$D charge-conserving free-fermion dynamics, which exhibits only area-law entanglement at finite measurement rates. We also show that the chiral DTDMs exhibit slow purification dynamics. When the system starts from a maximally mixed state, the DTDMs' entropy decays algebraically, accompanied by a vanishing Lyapunov gap, whereas each domain purifies on an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ timescale. Finally, we propose a physical picture for the long-time behavior of the DTDMs by treating the adaptive circuit model as a quantum cooling algorithm. Our results show that topological phases of adaptive dynamics can protect chiral modes on spacetime domain walls against repeated wavefunction collapse and Born-rule randomness.

title: Using a static spacetime subsystem code to calculate Floquet code distance
authors: Ethan Egger, Milad Marvian
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33337v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dynamical codes, including Floquet codes, can capture time-dependent phenomena in quantum error correction circuits that are absent from static stabilizer or subsystem codes, such as detecting regions and error propagation. They are also capable of preserving more logical qubits than corresponding schemes in which the same syndrome-extraction measurements are performed without being distributed over time. However, evaluating the performance of dynamical codes is more complicated than for static codes because error detection depends on when an error occurs within the measurement schedule. In this work, we introduce a mapping from the measurement sequence of a Floquet code to a static spacetime subsystem code and show that calculating the distance of a Floquet code can be reduced to calculating the distance of the corresponding static subsystem code. Crucially, our mapping preserves code distance, a property that is not guaranteed for general spacetime code mappings. This reduction converts the dynamical distance problem into a static subsystem code problem, substantially simplifying the analysis of Floquet measurement schedules and facilitating the evaluation of fault tolerance for new measurement schemes.

title: Quantum Copy Complexity of Testing Monotonicity and Other Properties
authors: Preksha Naik
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33340v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the sample complexity of testing monotonicity of Boolean functions when the tester is given only copies of the quantum function state $|\psi_f\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}|x,f(x)\rangle$. We give a tester with sample complexity $O\left(\min\left\{\frac{n}{\varepsilon^3}, \frac{n^{3/2}}{\varepsilon^2}\right\}\right)$, improving on the previous $\widetilde O(n^2/\varepsilon^2)$ upper bound of [CNS26]. We also prove the first nontrivial lower bounds for monotonicity testing from quantum function states, matching our upper bounds over a broad range of $\varepsilon$.
  Our upper bounds use two approaches. The first approach refines the Fourier-based tester of [CNS26] by handling high-influence functions separately, adapting an idea from [KMS18]. The second approach uses the classical path tester of [KMS18] by constructing a quantum observable whose expectation equals the path tester's violation probability.
  To prove the lower bounds, we place independent functions in mutually incomparable regions of the Boolean hypercube, building on the classical constructions of [BB16, CWX17]. We introduce a new argument for the quantum setting that replaces a fixed number of copies with a Poisson-distributed number of copies, allowing the contributions from different regions to be analyzed independently.
  This same framework also allows us to prove an $\Omega(n^2)$ lower bound for testing union-closedness and $2$-monotonicity from quantum function states.

title: Nitrogen-Vacancy Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy of $^{15}$N Spins in Potassium Nitrite Solution
authors: Sehrish Iqbal, Jitender Kumar, Suvechhya Lamichhane, Rupak Timalsina, Sy-Hwang Liou, Abdelghani Laraoui
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33360v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Nitrogen is essential in agricultural fertilizers, yet its nanoscale interfacial dynamics remain largely unexplored. Although quadrupolar broadening complicates $^{14}$N nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) detection, $^{15}$N (I=1/2) provides well-defined nuclear-spin signatures but remains challenging to detect at the nanoscale due to its low natural abundance and small gyromagnetic ratio. Here, we use a microfluidic quantum sensing platform based on shallow nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond to detect $^{15}$N NMR from KNO$_{3}$ solution at room temperature and in a low magnetic field regime. Within femtoliter-scale sensing volumes, we measure a magnetic-field variance of up to ~442 nT$^{2}$, ~43 times greater than the expected statistical polarization. The $^{15}$N spin correlation decays within ~500 $\mu\mathrm{s}$, mainly limited by the NV spin lattice relaxation time and not by the molecular diffusion of the KNO$_{3}$ molecules. This is consistent with the formation of a KNO$_{3}$ adsorption layer on the diamond surface, supported by surface characterization.

title: Electrical grid stabilisation through agent strategies : a mean-field game approach
authors: Loumi Gatouillat, Guillaume Roux, Dganit Meidan, C\'ecile Appert-Rolland, Cosimo Gorini, Denis Ullmo
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33386v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose and solve a minimal model based on mean-field game theory to study decentralized power consumption strategies to stabilize power grids. The mean-field Kuramoto description of an electrical network is coupled to agents with anticipatory capacity for decision making in energy consumption. Each agent minimizes an individual cost which includes both a financial part (cost induce by consumption and by power reservation) imposed by a central authority, and a (personal) non-monetary part. This elementary model of active oscillators is exactly solvable in the steady state regime. We show that the synchronized regime of the network can be significantly extended by the game.

title: Constructively Embedding Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Yucheng He, Todd A. Brun
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33389v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Implementing quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) requires more than favorable algebraic parameters: the interactions among data qubits and ancillas must also fit physical hardware. Surface codes map naturally onto two-dimensional arrays, but many quantum LDPC codes have Tanner graphs with nonlocal connections. We develop a constructive pipeline that maps a QECC's Tanner graph to the targeted hardware lattice in three stages (continuous embedding, grid assignment, and path routing). Continuous embeddings reveal the geometric structure of the code, including differences between stabilizer generator sets of the same code. The discrete stages produce explicit routed layouts that we can characterize and compare using proxy metrics for footprint, communication overhead, and congestion for syndrome extraction. We examine three continuous embedding methods: multidimensional scaling (distance-based), spectral embedding (Laplacian-based), and spring layout (force-based) for the first stage. Experiments across tested codes show how routing geometry, dimension, and scale selection affect the resulting costs. In ablation studies on the radius-2 (R2) HaPPY code, graph-aware methods for continuous embedding and the choice of path-routing algorithm matter more than the grid assignment under our chosen weights in the cost function. Changing the continuous embedding reveals a trade-off: MDS incurs greater communication overhead than spectral embedding over most tested scales, while spring layout can reduce communication overhead at intermediate scales but increases congestion and is less stable across scales.

title: How Many Keys Must a Quantum Computer Break to Take Over a Blockchain? A Quantum Nakamoto Coefficient for Fifteen Proof-of-Stake Networks
authors: Seyyed Mohammad Hassan Halataei
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33413v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Blockchains that run on proof of stake, among them Ethereum and Solana, are secured by a vote: a transaction becomes irreversible once computers holding two thirds of the deposited money have signed it. Each signature is made with a secret key whose public counterpart is permanently visible, and a large quantum computer could compute the secret from the public key. We ask a simple question: how many such keys would it have to break to take over the vote? We call the answer the quantum Nakamoto coefficient and measure it on live data from fifteen networks, collected on 15 November 2026. For fourteen of them, 2 to 18 keys are enough to break the network's security guarantee and 7 to 77 to control it outright; at one key every 12 minutes, the pace implied by recent resource estimates, a single quantum computer would defeat the guarantee of any of these networks in less than four hours and take full control in less than sixteen hours. Ethereum is far more robust, but a 2025 change that lets operators merge their deposits into fewer keys has cut the number of keys at its first threshold from about 465,000 to 7,682, a factor of 60. We derive a simple formula for this effect, and another for the small rotating committee on which wallets rely, and confirm both on the data. For fourteen of the fifteen networks, the first large quantum computer would be less than a day away from total control. Their validator signatures should therefore be migrated to post-quantum schemes before such a machine exists, since once it does, the time to respond is measured in hours.

title: Extracting Operational Entanglement from a Noise-Protected Many-Body System
authors: Bhavay Tyagi, Eric R. Bittner, Kevin E. Bassler
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33421v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can noisy dynamics generate entanglement that stays useful at long times? Under collective dephasing, a twelve-spin kicked Ising ring evolves from a uniform product state toward an entangled stationary state that is maximally mixed in the sector fixed by the ring's rotations and reflections. Gates and measurements within each half herald a spin pair that teleports an unknown qubit with a mean fidelity of 90.5\%. Simulations show that stronger noise correlations extend the time over which the ring yields pairs that beat the classical teleportation limit.

title: Estimating the Trotter error via phase analysis
authors: Maxime Dion, Benjamin D'Anjou
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33438v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Good Trotter error estimates are crucial to correctly assess the resources required to perform an approximate time evolution with a target accuracy. General bounds for finite-size quantum systems are found to be very loose in practice, and it is therefore highly desirable to improve on them. In this work, we analyze the Trotter error in terms of the spectrum of a phase operator that we construct from the Hamiltonian. In the limit of a small Trotter step size, we obtain an estimate of the Trotter error written in terms of a sum of nested commutators between terms of the Hamiltonian. The structure of this estimate allows us to naturally explain the looseness of general bounds. We show that even for a finite step size, our estimate typically remains more accurate than general bounds. Moreover, we argue that it becomes an upper bound for the Trotter error per step in the limit of a large number of steps, reflecting the destructive interference of the errors across steps. Our results provide useful practical heuristics for resource optimization in quantum simulations.

title: Extrinsic thermodynamic geometry, symmetry, and the cost of constraint
authors: Jordan R. Sawchuk, David A. Sivak
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Driving a stochastic system in finite time costs excess work; exactly how much depends on which system parameters, and hence which paths in distribution space, a controller can access. In the friction-tensor formalism for slow driving, the space of equilibrium distributions is a Riemannian manifold and constraints on a controller define submanifolds. Whether a constrained controller is forced onto suboptimal paths is a question of the extrinsic thermodynamic geometry of the submanifold, which we develop for discrete systems. We show that submanifolds with zero extrinsic curvature can be identified from symmetries of the transition network, before any optimization. A minimum-work protocol on such a submanifold is therefore stationary in the excess work even when the constraints are lifted. The stationarity of symmetric optima holds exactly, beyond slow driving. In the slow-driving regime, we show that the ambient curvature transverse to a symmetric submanifold determines whether nearby symmetry-broken protocols have lower excess work. This curvature, which separates into independent contributions from each pattern of symmetry breaking, thus acquires an operational meaning as a measure of the thermodynamic incentive to break a given symmetry. A thermodynamic comparison theorem provides an inexpensive test of local minimality that weighs the extremal curvatures along the symmetric protocol against its excess work. There is no need for such tests under certain convexity conditions on the transition rates and control parameters, which guarantee that a symmetric optimum is a global optimum. These results certify the global optimality of a five-parameter protocol previously observed to match 15-parameter full control of a four-spin Ising system, and explain why partial symmetry breaking is optimal for the same system under local-field control.

title: A Realistic End-to-End Runtime Crossover Estimation for Quantum-Enhanced Training of Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
authors: Maximilian Alexander Wolf, Alona Sakhnenko, Florian Geissler, Andrea Matic, Jeanette Miriam Lorenz
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33454v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) is one promising application domain for Quantum Computing (QC) speedups, but asymptotic complexity considerations often mask the actual engineering costs of actual end-to-end workflows. For the use case of training a linearized Neural Network with a Quantum Linear Solver, a provably favorable quantum scaling has been suggested. We present realistic resource estimates for this problem, accounting for data access, computation, and readout. Our analysis examines three increasingly complex benchmarking scenarios, under distinct sparsity-scaling assumptions, thereby enabling progressively more realistic resource estimates. We identify crossover regimes relative to classical methods and find that crossover points emerge only for very large problem sizes, long computation times, and highly restrictive output requirements. This work provides a blueprint for evaluating quantum-enhanced ML algorithms under realistic hardware constraints and help identifying the bottlenecks that must be overcome to approach industrial quantum utility.

title: NISQ Preparation of Conditional Thermal States for Precision Thermometry
authors: Emery Doucet, Reece Robertson, Nicholas Donatelli, Shou-I Tang, Sebastian Deffner, Akira Sone
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33461v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The ability to prepare thermal states on gate-based quantum computers is an important building block for quantum computation, both with regard to the implementation of certain classes of quantum algorithms as well as to the study of quantum thermodynamics in and out of equilibrium. A useful generalization of the standard notion of a thermal state which appears naturally in the study of quantum work distributions is the conditional thermal state, which is conditioned on the use of an accessible pointer basis associated with a measurement apparatus. Among other uses, it has been proven that conditional thermal states can outperform ordinary thermal states in quantum thermometry. In this work we demonstrate the preparation of conditional thermal states of few-qubit systems implemented on IonQ's cloud-based quantum computers across a range of temperatures. To validate their performance advantage in thermometry, we measure the sub-quantum Fisher information (a lower bound on the quantum Fisher information) of the prepared states, which can be computed via a constant-depth quantum circuit without tomography.

title: Optimal Controlled Quantum Instrument for Monitored Many-Body Dynamics
authors: Jimin Li
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33472v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-selecting rare trajectories of monitored quantum dynamics requires exponentially many repeated experiments. We extend Bayes' rule to monitored many-body dynamics and bias the quantum trajectories by nonlinear functions of the post-measurement state. For functions that are constant on the sets of a suitable finite partition of the post-measurement states, we construct a quantum instrument on the system and an additional register that produces the biased trajectories at the optimal rates without post-selection. This optimal controlled quantum instrument has a natural tensor-network representation as the left canonical form of the system--register tensors. We illustrate the construction with two examples: a precessing qubit, biased by its spin component along the field, and free fermions with gain and loss, biased by the particle number, where the biased trajectories undergo a phase transition. We also argue, under one assumption, that biasing a measured Majorana chain by its von Neumann entropy leads to entanglement transitions.

title: Infrared-absorption magnetometry in a diamond nanocavity: demonstration and limits at the nanoscale
authors: Nicholas J. Sorensen, Elham Zohari, Chris Coutts, Sean McNaney, Matteo Feder, Hadi Zadeh-Haghighi, Sigurd Fl{\aa}gan, Vinaya K. Kavatamane, Christoph Simon, Paul E. Barclay
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33481v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diamond quantum sensors promise both high spatial resolution and high sensitivity; however, conventional photoluminescence-based spin readout can be difficult to integrate efficiently. Infrared absorption by nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond provides a promising alternative, although the sensitivity of compact absorption-based sensors is limited by the short optical interaction length between the probe field and the NV ensemble. To overcome this limitation, we demonstrate, for the first time, singlet-absorption magnetometry using spin-dense diamond nanocavities. By probing cavity modes near the 1042 nm NV singlet transition, we observe spin-dependent cavity transmission and perform cavity-enhanced magnetic field sensing. We further develop and experimentally validate a model that accurately predicts the spin-dependent cavity response, describes the optimal operating conditions, and identifies the practical limitations of different optically detected magnetic resonance modalities. Together, these results establish cavity-enhanced singlet absorption as a scalable readout mechanism for integrated diamond quantum sensors and provide a practical framework for engineering next-generation nanophotonic diamond quantum magnetometers.

title: Statistical analysis of crossing beam speckle fields
authors: Ian D. Min-Roberts, Wojciech Rozmus, Pierre A. Michel
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33483v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Building on the statistical analysis of single beam speckles, this paper develops a statistical description of speckle fields formed by crossing laser beams. A formal definition of individual speckles and their domains allows us to quantify the effective size and abundance of speckles. For two crossing beams, the effective speckle size is derived from the local curvature of the intensity field, and the expected speckle abundance is found asymptotically with the Kac-Rice formula. Monte Carlo simulations of speckle abundance show excellent agreement with the theoretical abundance formula. The two beam speckle analysis is then applied to a symmetric quad beam configuration motivated by polarization smoothing and demonstrates that increasing the separation between beams reduces expected stimulated Brillouin scattering reflectivity from saturated speckles. The statistical model is then extended to an arbitrary number of beams using a coordinate free formulation to obtain the spectral density of laser driven electron density fluctuations.

title: Reducing T gates in product formulas with agent loops
authors: Luis Mantilla Calder\'on, J\'er\^ome F. Gonthier, Alex Zook, Kohei Nakaji, Taylor L. Patti, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33509v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum chemistry calculations on a fault-tolerant quantum computer usually require many $\text{T}$ gates. This cost depends on the simulation method and how precisely its rotations are implemented. In this paper, we used Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a large language model (LLM), in a coding-agent loop to optimize the structure and rotation-synthesis precision of product formulas (PFs) for quantum phase estimation (QPE). Each of five independent searches optimized a shared protocol across 115 HamLib molecular Hamiltonians spanning 4--16 qubits over 100 code mutations. The searches started from a calibrated, nested second-order PF with uniform synthesis precision. We minimized $T_{95}$, the estimated total $\text{T}$-gate cost including QPE queries and repeated attempts for $95\%$ success probability, while requiring chemical accuracy for every training Hamiltonian. We name the best protocol found error-limited optimized Trotter evolution (ELOTE). It achieves chemical accuracy for its training data and achieved median and geometric-mean $T_{95}$ reductions of $85.35\%$ and $84.82\%$, respectively. ELOTE combines contributions to the same Pauli string, uses a first-order PF, and varies synthesis precision with coefficient magnitude, Pauli support, and diagonal character. We also tested ELOTE on 76 larger Hamiltonians with 18--22 qubits, which met chemical accuracy in every case. For ten reaction energies, we further optimized a shared $\delta$-ELOTE protocol. It reduced geometric-mean $T_{95}$ by $58.90\%$ relative to ELOTE while preserving chemical accuracy for every signed reaction difference. These classically verified results show cost savings from shared protocols across molecules and reactions, and motivate similar searches in which energy measurements from quantum computers guide explorations in a coding-agent loop.

title: Robust Certification of Non-projective Qubit Measurements without Inputs
authors: Sumit Rout, Pawe{\l} Horodecki, Some Sankar Bhattacharya
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33559v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Positive-operator-valued measures (POVMs) beyond projective simulation (aka non-projective measurements) offer advantages over projective measurements, motivating their certification directly from observed statistics. Here, we show that this certification can be achieved robustly without input randomness, using only the joint outcome distribution of two measurement devices. We consider two spatially separated observers whose only shared resource is an uncharacterised two-qubit state. Each observer performs a local measurement. In the projective-simulable case, the measurement device privately randomises over qubit projective measurements and applies arbitrary classical post-processing to their outcomes. In the noiseless regime, we identify three- and four-outcome anti-correlations that certify that both local measurements lie beyond projective simulation. To establish noise robustness, we develop a non-linear covariance witness that combines the geometry of projective measurements with a contraction bound valid for every two-qubit state. For the correlations generated by identical qubit trine measurements or identical qubit SIC-POVM on noisy qubit singlet, we obtain exact critical white-noise fractions of (1/4) and (1/3), respectively. Below these thresholds, no pair of projective-simulable measurements on any two-qubit state can reproduce these correlations. We present explicit projective simulations that attain the thresholds and cover the remaining noise range. Finally, the same method yields a strictly positive noise tolerance for certification whenever both observers apply the same extremal qubit POVM with three or four non-zero effects to a depolarised qubit singlet. These results establish a general analytic framework for certifying non-projective qubit measurement resources without input randomness.

title: The Phases of Hierarchy
authors: Gerard McCaul
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33566v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We develop a dynamical phase theory of hierarchy, in which depth decides whether a population of size $N$ that revises its own environment can correct it without overcorrecting. The statistics that let a large majority detect a small bias - the basis of the Condorcet jury theorem - also make its response grow as $\sqrt{N}$. Fed back into the environment it is judging, this sharpening destabilises the matched state through a flip bifurcation at a critical loop gain, which we obtain analytically for a class of models we term adaptive normal forms. We show that this instability can be attenuated by hierarchical layering, requiring a depth scaling logarithmically with $N$. This recovers known logarithmic bounds in organisational economics directly from dynamic stability conditions. Hierarchical depth carries its own costs however, and by analysing the signal chain transmission up the hierarchy we show that beyond a finite depth no correction reaches the top before its deadline, and that below it the cost of arrival grows exponentially with depth. A hierarchy that is too flat therefore oscillates and one that is too deep cannot be steered in time, leaving a bounded window of depth between an unstable flat phase and a frozen inertial phase. We further show that these results can be generalised by treating each layer as a real-space renormalisation step, classifying aggregation rules by how they transmit bias. This establishes a connection between these dynamic results to attention in Transformers, where a residual update is diffusion on the token graph and depth plays the role of scale. Finally we show these phase boundaries are observable in finite sampling, and propose measurements which may characterise the proposed phases in real adaptive systems.

title: Equilibrium finiteness and Saari's conjecture for the planar circular restricted N-body problem
authors: Qinglong Zhou
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We establish two results for planar Newtonian centers in uniform rotation. First, the associated quadratic-plus-Newtonian amended potential has finitely many equilibria for every finite configuration of at least two distinct centers with positive masses. Second, every collision-free planar test-particle motion with constant amended potential, equivalently constant rotating-frame speed, is stationary in the rotating frame. When the centers are primary bodies in a circular relative equilibrium, this proves the amended-potential form of Saari's conjecture for the restricted \(N\)-body problem.

title: Symmetry-Aware Residual Learning of Few-Body Molecular Wave Functions
authors: Meital Bojan, Mikhail Maslov, Jing-Lun Li, Alex M. Bronstein, Mikhail Lemeshko
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ultracold polar molecules are a highly controllable platform for engineering quantum matter, but modeling their few-body properties remains computationally challenging. Their anisotropic long-range interactions and rich internal structure lead to high-dimensional eigenvalue problems for which conventional grid-based solvers are largely restricted to two-molecule systems. To address this limitation, we introduce a physics-informed neural variational method that exploits known physical structure of the molecular wave function. Our key idea is to factor the wave function into analytic and neural components. The analytic component encodes rotational symmetry and asymptotic decay, while the neural residual learns the remaining intermediate-range behavior. This decomposition reduces the effective dimensionality of the problem without relying on ad hoc approximations or problem-specific discretization grids. We benchmark our method against high-accuracy two-molecule solvers and recover both ground and excited bound states with mean relative errors below 0.01%. We further demonstrate the method's applicability to three-body systems by computing field-linked trimer ground-state energies in percent-level agreement with an independent grid-based calculation. This provides a systematic route to larger molecular systems and opens opportunities to study correlations and dynamics in interacting quantum matter.

title: A scalable dense silicon qubit architecture with logical operations
authors: Masahiro Tadokoro, Tetsuo Kodera
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33590v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires a large number of physical qubits to encode logical qubits with sufficiently low error rates. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform because of their small footprint, compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing technologies, and demonstrated high-fidelity operations. However, realizing a scalable architecture that supports quantum error correction, qubit transport, wiring, and logical gate operations remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture designed to support large-scale FTQC. The architecture consists of qubit memories, data qubit lanes, and cross junctions. Qubit memories store logical qubits encoded using the rotated surface code and support logical single-qubit operations. Data qubit lanes enable high-speed one-dimensional spin shuttling for connectivity between logical qubits, while cross junctions provide routing functionality and implement transversal logical CNOT gates. Using experimentally demonstrated silicon spin qubit parameters, we evaluate logical error rates as a function of code distance and estimate that a code distance of at least 21 is required to achieve logical error rates below $10^{-10}$ per syndrome cycle. We further analyze wiring constraints based on CMOS-compatible multiplexed control schemes and show that, with optimized wiring efficiency, more than 120,000 logical qubits could be integrated on a 100 mm $\times$ 100 mm chip. These results provide a practical roadmap toward large-scale FTQC based on silicon spin qubit technology.

title: Numerical Studies of Ground State Atomic Parity Violation Measurements in Cesium
authors: Chunya Wang, Matthew Summers, Jonah A. Quirk, Diego Garcia, Carol E. Tanner, D. S. Elliott
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We report results of numerical simulations of an ongoing measurement designed to measure the electric dipole (E1) transition moment between hyperfine components of the ground state of atomic cesium. This E1 moment is non-zero solely due to nuclear weak interactions between the nucleons, leading to a nuclear anapole moment of the cesium nucleus. Through these simulations, we explore the effect on the microwave spectrum of a static transverse magnetic field, a spatial offset of the atomic beam from the axis of the radio-frequency (rf) cavity, the angular tilt of the rf cavity, and the ac Stark shift by the Raman-coupling beams used to generate the initial superposition state between ground state components. The results of these simulations help place limits on the experimental parameters, and help guide the future experimental procedures.

title: High-Dimensional Single-Photon Frequency Conversion for Orbital Angular Momentum Comb State
authors: Sheng-Qiang Jia, Hao Sheng, Zhiming Qing, Li Fan, Jianping Ding, Jia-Min Xu, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33642v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The orbital angular momentum (OAM) degree of freedom provides an important resource for constructing high-dimensional optical quantum information systems. However, the generation of high-dimensional single-photon OAM comb state and its high-fidelity frequency conversion remain challenging due to limited spatial modulation resolution, imperfect mode matching, and finite nonlinear conversion efficiency. Here, we proposed and experimentally demonstrated a scalable scheme for the generation and frequency conversion of high-dimensional single-photon OAM comb state. We prepared a single-photon OAM comb state with a dimension of up to 128, achieving a fidelity of 0.787 between the reconstructed and target states and an effective dimension of 100. Furthermore, using the sum-frequency generation, we demonstrated the frequency upconversion of single-photon high-dimensional OAM comb state from the communication band to a visible wavelength of 520 nm, while verifying the preservation of both the OAM mode distribution and phase information through density matrix reconstruction. Our work established a versatile platform for the generation, manipulation, and characterization of high-dimensional OAM comb states, with potential applications in cross-band quantum information transfer, high-capacity quantum communication, and high-dimensional quantum networks.

title: Amatlas: A 2D Array Architecture for Union-Find Decoding Without Global Coordination
authors: Takuya Kasamura, Leo Itoh, Seita Tsuboi, Hidetsugu Irie, Junichiro Kadomoto
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33665v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-time decoding of the surface code is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and scaling the decoder to large code distances in hardware remains a challenge. The locality of Union-Find (UF) decoding makes it a leading candidate for such a decoder in distributed hardware. Prior distributed UF decoders, however, map the three-dimensional decoding graph onto an array of processing elements (PEs) under a central controller that synchronizes all PEs at every stage, and a three-dimensional array of PEs scales poorly on planar hardware. This paper presents Amatlas, a two-dimensional PE array for UF decoding that operates without a central controller. Amatlas assigns one PE to each stabilizer on the two-dimensional qubit lattice and stores the states of all measurement rounds in the local memory of the PE, so every link connects adjacent PEs in the array. Every PE advances on every clock cycle without array-wide synchronization, and the clock is the only global signal of the array. Under circuit-level noise, the RTL implementation of Amatlas fits a VCU129 FPGA up to a code distance of 25, where the average decoding time is 462 ns per round at a physical error rate of 0.1%. Amatlas achieves a threshold of 0.72%, compared with 0.78% reported for UF decoding under the same noise model.

title: Dimensional crossover to a slow disordered spin bath below the mean spin spacing
authors: Chikara Shinei
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33699v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How thin must a layer of spins be to act as a two-dimensional bath? For nitrogen spins around an NV$^-$ centre in diamond, a cluster expansion with flip-flopping outer spins gives a crossover near the mean spin spacing. Thin layers follow two-dimensional scaling with a prefactor six to seven times that of bulk. Without hyperfine disorder the crossover remains but the step is under three: the disorder leaves each spin almost no resonant partner. Flip-flops allow several milliseconds, so another process must set the measured 0.5 ms; nitrogen spin-lattice relaxation is consistent.

title: On-Demand Tailoring of High-Dimensional Orbital Angular Momentum States via a Phase-Only Hologram
authors: Hao Sheng, Zi-Shuo Wang, Sheng-Qiang Jia, Zi-Mo Cheng, Li Fan, Jianping Ding, Jia-Min Xu, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33704v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Photonic orbital angular momentum (OAM) provides a naturally discrete and unbounded Hilbert space for high-dimensional encoding and has emerged as a powerful degree of freedom for advanced information processing. On-demand tailoring of both the amplitude and phase profiles of high-dimensional OAM states is essential for numerous applications, particularly in quantum information science. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate an efficient method for achieving such on-demand tailoring using a purely phase-only modulation scheme. The measured fidelity remains above 80% even for a 128-dimensional state, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Compared with previous techniques, our method achieves significantly higher generation efficiency, and this advantage becomes more pronounced as the dimensionality increases. Moreover, our approach substantially reduces experimental complexity while maintaining precise control, thereby offering a practical and scalable solution for high-dimensional OAM state engineering in both classical and quantum information processing.

title: A nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme II: multi-frequency radiation transport
authors: Hongyu Liu, Xiaojian Yang, Xing Ji, Jianxian Qiu, Kun Xu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33718v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional discrete ordinate methods are widely used for thermal radiative transfer, but their fixed number of angular degrees of freedom (DoFs) incurs unnecessary computational cost near equilibrium. We therefore develop a nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme (NCUGKS) for multi-frequency radiation transport. The scheme preserves the mul tiscale capability of UGKS through interface evolution that couples transport and collision. Radiation intensity is expanded in an orthonormal basis of the discrete angular space. The expansion coefficients serve as angular DoFs, with their number adapted independently to local nonequilibrium in each cell, frequency group, and quadrant. At each time step, the coefficients to be evolved are selected using the exponentially decayed contribution from the previous step and the requirements of interface transport. The selected coefficients are advanced by the finite volume scheme and corrected to match the macroscopic radiation energy before higher-degree coefficients are discarded according to the prescribed relative tail tolerance. Therefore, in the optically thick limit, the resulting representation retains only one angular DoF per quadrant. Numerical tests spanning different optical regimes show close agreement with reference solutions, validating its accuracy. Furthermore, in terms of memory and computational efficiency, the proposed method reduces memory by factors from 21.7 to 154.0 and achieves speedups from 24.87 to 257.9 compared with the original discrete ordinate UGKS. NCUGKS thus provides the ability to accurately simulate multiscale ra diative transfer with reduced memory and computational costs. The proposed approach also offers a framework for adapting angular degrees of freedom in other discrete ordinate methods.

title: Deep-learning-enabled rapid spatially multiplexed wavefront sensing with a thin diffuser
authors: Ming Xue, Shijie Wei, Shulei Zhao, Zhuojia Shi, Tengfei Wu, Xiaopeng Shao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33724v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional wavefront sensing typically measures aberrations along a single guide-star direction, limiting the correction of field-dependent aberrations over a wide field of view. Spatial multiplexing with a thin diffuser enables simultaneous measurements across multiple isoplanatic patches, but the computational cost of reconstruction makes it difficult to track changing aberrations. We propose a deep-learning approach that combines recurrent all-pairs field transforms for displacement estimation with Zernike coefficient regression. Experimental results show that the method accurately reconstructs multiple wavefronts from a single speckle pattern and reduces three-channel reconstruction time from 2801.6 ms with conventional digital image correlation (DIC) to 23.1 ms. The reconstructed wavefronts agreed more closely with sequential single-channel references than those obtained by multiplexed DIC, and simulations showed that Zernike regression was more robust to noise than direct gradient integration. These results suggest a path toward dynamic wide-field aberration sensing and high-speed adaptive optics.

title: When Malus' Law Meets the Wigner-Bell Inequality: Violation by Nonseparable Classical Light
authors: Xiao-Feng Qian
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33729v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bell-type inequalities are commonly associated with quantum nonlocality, yet their mathematical structure also reflects more general constraints on the joint probability distributions assigned to measurements performed in different contexts. Here we examine this distinction through the Wigner--Bell inequality using a classical optical field with two nonseparable degrees of freedom. Starting from a subsystem response-factorization assumption, we derive a Wigner-type probability bound requiring the pairwise measurement statistics to be compatible with a single nonnegative global joint distribution. For a classically nonseparable optical field, the corresponding joint probabilities are represented directly by normalized joint intensities and obey Malus' law. We show that these Malus-law probabilities violate the Wigner--Bell bound over a finite range of analyzer settings. The violation does not imply spatial nonlocality or a failure of classical electrodynamics. Rather, it demonstrates the incompatibility of context-dependent optical projection statistics with the global probability assignment underlying the Wigner construction. We further derive an extended Wigner-Bell bound for general imperfect correlations and propose an interferometric experiment for reconstructing the required joint probabilities from intensity measurements. These results provide a transparent optical realization of the probabilistic structure behind Bell-type inequalities and help distinguish consequences of Hilbert-space structure, nonseparability, and measurement context from those specifically associated with quantum nonlocality.

title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More
authors: Masayuki Miyamoto
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33730v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. For general edge weights, the classical dynamic programs of Bellman and of Held and Karp solve TSP on $n$ cities in $O^*(2^n)$ time. To date, no $\Oh(c^n)$-time classical algorithm is known for any $c<2$. Combining Grover search with the dynamic programming technique, Ambainis et al. (SODA 2019) introduced a quantum algorithm with running time $O^*(1.7274^n)$, which is still the best known quantum time bound.
  In this work, we improve the running time to $O^*(1.70961^n)$. The core idea of our algorithm is to combine the framework of Ambainis et al. with the extremal set-system framework, which was recently used for classical space-time tradeoffs of TSP by Jabal Ameli, Nederlof and Wang (FOCS 2026) and Dallant and Kozma (FOCS 2026). To obtain our upper bound, we decompose the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of different sizes, for which, based on the idea of set-systems, the optimal values are computed using dynamic programming with small success probability and use amplitude amplification. Using the same idea, we also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP, improving the previous results of Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant (arXiv:2607.12374). Finally, we obtain the same quantum upper bounds for several other related problems.

title: Carrier relaxation confines the Bogdanov--Takens degeneracy of an optically injected semiconductor laser
authors: A. Mart\'in-Ruiz, E. Chan-L\'opez, Carlos Antonio Mar\'in-Mendoza
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33746v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optically injected semiconductor lasers are forced nonlinear oscillators whose locking boundaries are organized by codimension-two points. We ask which property of the carrier balance permits or forbids a Bogdanov--Takens (BT) point in the standard three-dimensional rate equations. Taking the carrier inversion $n$ as distinguished observable, the rate that enters the spectral conditions is the slope of the gain--loss balance, $\xi=\partial\dot n/\partial n=-2\Gamma/\kappa$, where $\Gamma$ is the damping of the relaxation oscillation and $\kappa=1+2Bn$ the normalized stimulated-emission factor. The two BT conditions become affine in $\xi$ and imply the exact sum rule $K^{2}=I[1-(1+\kappa)I]$ between injection amplitude $K$ and intracavity intensity $I$. The product of the two relaxation eigenvalues that survive at a saddle-node is bounded below by $1-16\Gamma^{2}$, so that no BT point exists for $\Gamma<1/4$, whatever $B$, the linewidth enhancement factor, the injection strength and the detuning; below this barrier every contact between Hopf and saddle-node curves is a fold--Hopf point. For $B=0$ the barrier is completed to an exact existence criterion. We prove that the unfolding of a BT point by injection strength and detuning is transversal if and only if two explicit curves cross transversally in the plane of locked states; for $B=0$ this is a simple root of an explicit function, and transversality fails exactly at the existence threshold. Two BT points at $\Gamma=1/2$, $\alpha=2$ are verified to be generic, and the contacts between Hopf and saddle-node curves are classified into fold--Hopf, BT and nilpotent triple-zero points.

title: Structure theorem for quantum limit cycle attractors: A geometric path-integral approach
authors: Nana Siddhartha
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33776v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show a Structure Theorem for an arbitrary separable quantum system (\(\dim\mathcal{H}\leq\aleph_0\)) that is coupled, through a symmetric bidirectional phase interface, to a self-sustaining phase-oscillator environment. Under the assumptions of \(U(1)\) covariance, instantaneous Lindblad bounded positivity, and the existence of an entrainable periodic attractor, the reduced generator is forced into a universal operator structure consisting of a state-dependent coherent recoil together with single-quantum feedback. Positivity further imposes a sharp dimensional dichotomy: purely dissipative gain saturation is forbidden in finite dimensions by trace-norm contraction, so coherent feedback is mandatory for qubits and qudits, whereas unbounded ladder algebras permit purely dissipative saturation. Expanding the general feedback functionals to leading order in the coupling recovers a canonical polynomial master equation that remains completely positive and trace-preserving in every dimension and combines additively with ordinary linear Lindblad channels. An accompanying Inverse Coupling Theorem shows that an autonomous periodic orbit can be sustained only when the interaction manifold has non-trivial fundamental group \(\pi_1(\mathcal{M})=\mathbb{Z}\), thereby isolating the sinusoidal \(U(1)\)-covariant phase coupling as the generic mechanism. The resulting implementation is realized explicitly for a single qubit, a bipartite two-qubit system, and a bosonic Fock space.

title: Existence of single-resonance parametric bound states in the continuum: System of Schr\"odinger equations
authors: Xiuchen Yu, Ya Yan Lu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33784v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A bound state in the continuum (BIC) is an eigenmode of a linear wave system with its eigen-frequency embedded in the radiation continuum of scattering states. At the frequency of a BIC, scattering problems with given incident waves from infinity lose uniqueness. Due to their close connection with strong resonance effects, BICs have found many useful applications in classical and quantum wave systems. Existence theories of BICs have been established for some cases involving the so-called symmetry-protected BICs, Friedrich-Wintgen BICs, and Fabry-Perot BICs. The single-resonance parametric BICs (srp-BICs) are another important class of BICs. Such a BIC emerges from a single resonant state through tuning a real parameter. Using a simple system of two one-dimensional Schr\"odinger equations, we demonstrate the formation of srp-BICs and establish a rigorous existence theory.

title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference
authors: Yixiong Chen
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33806v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.

title: A bright source of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs based on beam-like Type-II SPDC
authors: Ming Zhang, Zhiming Qing, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Jianping Ding, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33852v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bright sources of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs are increasingly required for the rapid advancement of quantum technologies. However, simultaneously achieving high brightness and high-dimensional spatial entanglement through spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a bright source of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs using beam-like Type-II SPDC in a $\beta$-barium borate crystal. Compared with a conventional collinear Type-I source, it exhibits a $\sim$1.56-fold enhancement in the detected single-photon count rate and a $\sim$1.45-fold enhancement in the coincidence count rate. Measurements of position correlations and momentum anti-correlations certify at least 62-dimensional spatial entanglement within a 121-dimensional basis. These correlations are further exploited to demonstrate quantum imaging in both the position and momentum domains. These characteristics make the source a practical resource for high-dimensional photonic quantum technologies.

title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm for the Generalised Geography Game
authors: Mriganka Sandilya, Shibdas Roy
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33853v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Generalized Geography Game ($GGG$) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a directed graph, where players alternately move a token along edges without revisiting previously visited vertices. In the existing literature, determining whether an arbitrary position in a graph is a winning position for either player is a well-known $PSPACE$-complete decision problem. Certain formulations of $GGG$ have been shown to fall outside the $PSPACE$-complete complexity class. While $PSPACE$-complete problems are believed to take exponential time for classical computation, quantum computation offers new possibilities. In this work, we present a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time ($BQP$) algorithm for solving the $GGG$ problem. The proposed algorithm runs in time $O(N^{2}/\epsilon^{6})$, which is polynomial in the input size $N$, and achieves bounded error with $\epsilon = O(1/\mathrm{poly}(N))$. This result demonstrates the potential of quantum algorithms to efficiently solve combinatorial game problems that are traditionally considered computationally hard in the classical setting.

title: Reproducible distributions of energy-relaxation times in superconducting qubits from broadband SWAP spectroscopy
authors: Joaquin Minguzzi, John Clai Owens, Maximilien F. Debbas, Ana Vald\'es-Curiel, Ming-Han Chou, Haifeng Qiao, Shahriar Aghaeimeibodi, Oskar Painter, Matthew H. Matheny, Loren J. Swenson
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33854v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The distribution of the qubit energy-relaxation time (T1) in a superconducting quantum processor affects its logical error rates. However, reports on qubit fabrication quality focus on the median or best-case T1 from measurements that are not reproducible due to resonant coupling to two-level system (TLS) defects whose frequencies fluctuate in time. Here, we sweep the frequency f01 of a flux-tunable qubit over several GHz with SWAP spectroscopy, quoting the quality factor Q = 2 pi f01 T1 to make T1 comparable across frequencies. We show that the cumulative distribution of Q pooled over the sweep is reproducible across four thermal cycles spanning 326 days, up to the reshuffling of strongly coupled TLSs. In contrast to repeated measurements at a single frequency, the medians of the broadband Q distributions spread by an order of magnitude less over 3 days. The distance between the cumulative distributions of repeats comes close to its sampling floor only for the broadband sweeps. The broadband Q distribution further resolves small coherence differences between identically designed qubits on two dies of the same wafer. These results establish the broadband Q distribution as a reproducible metric for qubit fabrication quality.

title: How Many Autonomous Encoded Qubits Force an Isotropic Noise Response?
authors: Xu Chen, Xue Ma
abstract:
arXiv:2611.33864v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Depolarizing noise scales trace distances by a common factor. An encoded qubit is autonomous if its reduced input state determines its output. For $D=2^n\ge4$, autonomy forces this isotropy at a sharp threshold of $(D^2+5)/3$ generic encodings, two more than state tomography requires. For Pauli noise, one generic encoding suffices. With one-bit readouts and no quantum memory or reference, switching encodings cuts the worst-case cost for the Pauli test by a factor of $D$, up to logarithms. For any family, a channel with leakage $O(D^{-3/2})$ can transmit one bit perfectly and erase another.
